title: Section 1 (Lines 1–11)
subtitle: Jupiter and Mercury arrive in disguise

words.p: noun · Nominative singular — subject of vēnit.
words.x: King of the gods. Ovid puts him first for impact — the divine visitor opens the story.

words.p: adverb · Adverb of place (motion towards), with vēnit.
words.x: Points to the destination — Phrygia, where the story is set.

words.p: noun · Ablative singular — ablative of manner: “in the form of”, with mortālī.
words.x: 5th-declension noun (like rēs, diēs).

words.p: adjective · Ablative singular, agreeing with speciē.
words.x: From mors (“death”) — literally “subject to death”, i.e. human.

words.p: preposition · Preposition governing parente.
words.x: Don’t confuse with the conjunction cum (“when, since”) — here it takes the ablative and means “with”.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, attached to cum.
words.x: -que tacks onto the end of a word and joins more tightly than et.

words.p: noun · Ablative singular, with cum.
words.x: Here = Jupiter, the “parent” of Mercury, who travels at his side.

rows.en: Jupiter came here in human form and, with his father, (came)

words.p: verb · 3rd person singular, perfect indicative active: “(he) came”.
words.x: Perfect tense — the long ē of vēnit distinguishes it from present venit.

words.p: noun · Nominative singular (Greek 1st declension) — the second subject of vēnit.
words.x: A patronymic: it names Mercury through his ancestor Atlas — grand, epic-sounding diction.

words.p: participle · Perfect passive participle, ablative plural, with ālīs — together an ablative absolute: “with his wings laid aside”.
words.x: Forms the ablative absolute positīs ālīs.

words.p: adjective · Nominative singular masculine, describing Mercury (Atlantiadēs).
words.x: A poetic compound: cādūceus (herald’s wand) + ferō (“carry”).

words.p: noun · Ablative plural, in the ablative absolute with positīs.
words.x: Mercury’s winged sandals — taken off so the gods can pass as ordinary mortals.

rows.en: the wand-bearing descendant of Atlas, having set aside his wings.

words.p: numeral · Indeclinable adjective, with domōs (accusative plural).
words.x: “A thousand” often just means “countless” — here it stresses how many doors are shut.

words.p: noun · Accusative plural (domōs) — object of adiēre.
words.x: 4th-declension noun with some 2nd-declension endings; accusative plural is domōs.

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural perfect, adiēre = adiērunt (syncopated): “they approached”.
words.x: Compound of ad + eō (“go”). Poets often shorten -ērunt to -ēre.

words.p: noun · Accusative singular — object of petentēs.
words.x: Here “a place (to stay)”.

words.p: noun · Accusative singular (requiem) — object of petentēs.
words.x: From re- + quiēs (“rest”): the weary travellers want somewhere to stop.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, joining locum and requiem.
participle · Present active participle, nominative plural — describing the two gods: “seeking”.
words.x: petō can also mean “attack, aim at” (a military sense); here it is the gentler “seek”.

rows.en: They approached a thousand houses, seeking a place and rest:

words.p: numeral · Indeclinable adjective, with domōs.
words.x: The phrase mīlle domōs is repeated from line 3 — the same houses now shut their doors.

words.p: noun · Accusative plural — object of clausēre.
verb · 3rd person plural perfect, clausēre = clausērunt (syncopated): “(they) shut”.
words.x: The subject is serae (“bolts”) — so literally the bolts shut the houses.

words.p: noun · Nominative plural — subject of clausēre.
words.x: Making the bolts the subject is vivid: the houses themselves seem to slam shut.

words.p: adverb · Adverb marking a contrast.
words.x: The turning point: after every door is shut, one will open.

words.p: numeral · Nominative singular feminine — “one (cottage)”, subject of recēpit.
words.x: Irregular: genitive ūnīus, dative ūnī. Here “one alone” welcomes them.

words.p: verb · 3rd person singular perfect: “(it) received (them)”.
words.x: Compound of re- + capiō (“take”); the regular verb for welcoming guests.

rows.en: However, one received (them), a small (one), it is true, covered with stalks — bars shut a thousand houses.

words.p: adjective · Nominative singular feminine, describing the cottage.
words.x: Its small size is stressed — the contrast is with the great welcome inside.

words.p: adverb · Adverb, conceding a point.
words.x: A concession: yes, the cottage is small — but (the contrast follows).

words.p: noun · Ablative plural — ablative of means with tēcta: “covered with straw”.
words.x: Humble thatching material — a poor person’s roof.

words.p: conjunction · Conjunction, joining stipulīs and cannā.
noun · Ablative singular — ablative of means with tēcta.
words.x: Marsh reed, used with straw to thatch the roof.

words.p: participle · Perfect passive participle, nominative singular feminine, describing the cottage: “(having been) roofed”.
words.x: The noun tēctum (“roof, house”) comes from this verb.

words.p: adjective · Ablative singular feminine, agreeing with cannā.
words.x: From palūs (“marsh, swamp”) — the reeds grow in the wetlands.

words.p: conjunction · Conjunction marking a contrast.
words.x: Shifts the focus from the building to the good people living inside it.

words.p: adjective · Nominative singular feminine, describing Baucis.
words.x: pietās — duty to gods, family and guests — is the great Roman virtue, flagged here at once.

words.p: noun · Nominative singular (Greek) — one of the subjects.
words.x: The old woman of the cottage; her Greek name suits the Phrygian setting.

words.p: noun · Nominative singular, in apposition to Baucis.
words.x: A 4th-declension feminine noun — one of a small group (cf. manus, domus).

words.p: adjective · Ablative singular, with aetāte: “equal in age”.
words.x: A poetic word for pār (“equal”) — the couple are perfectly matched.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, joining Baucis and Philēmōn.
noun · Ablative singular — ablative of respect with parīlī: “equal in age”.
noun · Nominative singular (Greek) — the second subject.
words.x: Baucis’s husband; the two are always named together.

rows.en: But the dutiful old woman Baucis, and Philemon, equal in age,

words.p: pronoun · Ablative singular feminine, with casā: “in that cottage”.
words.x: A demonstrative. It is repeated (illā … illā) to dwell on the one place that was their whole life.

words.p: verb · sunt … iūnctī = perfect passive, 3rd person plural: “(they) were united”.
words.x: sunt + the participle iūnctī together make the perfect passive — “were joined (in marriage)”.

words.p: noun · Ablative plural, with iuvenālibus: “in (their) youthful years”.
participle · Perfect passive participle, nominative plural masculine, with sunt: “united”.
words.x: iungō is the usual verb for joining a couple in marriage (cf. coniūnx, “spouse”).

words.p: adjective · Ablative plural, with annīs.
words.x: From iuvenis (“a young person”) — they married when young.

words.p: pronoun · Ablative singular feminine, with casā: “in that (same) cottage”.
words.x: The second illā — they married there and grew old there, in the one place.

rows.en: were united in their younger years in that cottage, (and)

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural perfect, cōnsenūēre = cōnsenuērunt (syncopated): “they grew old together”.
words.x: The prefix con- (“together”) is the point: they aged side by side, as one.

words.p: noun · Ablative singular, with illā: “in that cottage”.
words.x: A casa is a humble dwelling — very different from a grand domus.

words.p: noun · Accusative singular — object of the gerund fatendō.
words.x: From pauper (“poor”). Roman moralists admired honest poverty borne with dignity.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction, linking the clauses.
gerund · Gerund, ablative (fatendō) — ablative of means: “by acknowledging”.
words.x: A deponent verb: passive in form but active in meaning.

rows.en: grew old together in that cottage, and by acknowledging

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural perfect, effēcēre = effēcērunt (syncopated): “(they) made (it)”.
words.x: Compound of ex- + faciō (“make”). With levem: “made (it) light”.

words.p: adjective · Accusative singular, predicative with effēcēre: “made (it) light”.
words.x: Opposite of gravis (“heavy”). Here it means easy to bear — their poverty weighs nothing on them.

words.p: conjunction · Conjunction, negating the phrase inīquā mente.
words.x: nec … ferendō = “and by bearing it with no resentful spirit”.

words.p: adjective · Ablative singular feminine, with mente.
words.x: From in- (“not”) + aequus (“level, fair”) — literally “not level”; here “resentful”.

words.p: noun · Ablative singular — ablative of manner: “with (a) … attitude”.
words.x: nec inīquā mente = “with no bitter frame of mind”.

words.p: gerund · Gerund, ablative (ferendō) — ablative of means: “by bearing (it)”.
words.x: An irregular verb. Here “bear, put up with” — they endure poverty without complaint.

rows.en: their poverty and made it light by bearing it not with an unfair mind.

words.p: conjunction · Conjunction joining this sentence to the last.

words.m: it matters, it makes a difference
words.p: verb · Impersonal verb, 3rd person singular present: “it matters”.
words.x: Used impersonally (no personal subject): nec refert = “and it makes no difference”.

words.p: noun · Accusative plural — object of requīrās in the indirect question.
words.x: The head of a household of slaves — but here there are none to look for.

words.p: adverb · Adverb of place.
words.x: = “in that cottage”.

words.p: noun · Accusative plural — object of requīrās.
words.x: Paired with dominōs: there is neither master nor servant to be found.

words.p: particle · Enclitic question particle, attached to famulōs.
words.x: dominōs … famulōsne = “whether masters or servants”.

words.p: verb · 2nd person singular present subjunctive: “(whether) you look for”.
words.x: Compound of re- + quaerō (“seek”). The subjunctive suits the indirect question.

rows.en: And it does not matter whether you look for masters there or slaves:

words.p: adjective · Nominative singular feminine, with domus.
words.x: Irregular: genitive tōtīus, dative tōtī.

words.p: noun · Nominative singular — “the whole household”.
words.x: Here domus means the household (the people), not the building.

words.p: numeral · Nominative plural masculine — “the two (of them)”.
words.x: An irregular numeral. duo sunt = “are (just) the two”.

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural present: “(they) are”.
words.x: tōta domus duo sunt = “the two are the whole household”.

words.p: pronoun · Nominative plural masculine — “the same (people)”.
words.x: From is + -dem. The same two are both masters and servants — equals in everything.

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural present: “they obey”.
words.x: Don’t confuse with pariō (“give birth”) or appāreō (“appear”).

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction (pārentque).
words.x: The pair -que … -que (“both … and”) links obeying and commanding into one idea.

words.p: verb · 3rd person plural present: “they command”.
words.x: Set against pārent: they both obey and give the orders — the paradox of two equals.

words.p: conjunction · Enclitic conjunction (iubentque).

rows.en: the two are the whole house, they both obey and command.

notes.label: Initial Position
notes.body: The first word of the passage is the king of the gods. Ovid announces divine presence immediately — this is not a story about ordinary travellers. Placing Iuppiter emphatically at the start mirrors the fanfare of epic openings.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The emphatic initial position of Iuppiter immediately establishes the divine presence and signals the theoxeny (divine visitation) motif that will structure the narrative."

notes.label: Patronymic
notes.body: Mercury is named not as Mercury but as "descendant of Atlas" — a Greek-style patronymic borrowed from Homer. Ovid uses it to elevate the register: this is proper epic diction, lending grandeur to a story set in a humble cottage.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The patronymic Atlantiadēs employs epic naming conventions, lending the domestic narrative an elevated, Homeric register while identifying Mercury through his divine genealogy."

notes.label: Compound Epithet
notes.body: A compound adjective that immediately identifies Mercury through his famous attribute, the caduceus. These compound epithets are a hallmark of epic style — one word doing double duty, naming and characterising simultaneously.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The compound epithet caducifer identifies Mercury through his divine attribute while employing a typically poetic word-formation that elevates the register."

notes.label: Ablative Absolute
notes.body: An ablative absolute compressing a whole subordinate clause into two words. Mercury has removed his winged sandals to pass as mortal. The gods are incognito — only the reader knows who is really standing at each door.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The ablative absolute positīs ālīs economically conveys the god's transformation, suggesting conscious concealment of divine markers for the mortal disguise."

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.trans: a thousand houses… a thousand houses
notes.body: The same phrase — mīlle domōs — recurs with opposite verbs: approached, then shut. The repetition makes the universal rejection feel crushing. Every single house said no. The parallelism of language mirrors the parallelism of the situation.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The anaphora of mīlle domōs emphasises the comprehensive rejection the disguised gods face, highlighting the community's failure of hospitality through emphatic repetition."

notes.label: Syncopated Perfect
notes.body: A shortened (syncopated) perfect — adiērunt compressed to adiēre for metrical elegance. These syncopated forms are a feature of Latin poetry. The same technique appears with clausēre and cōnsenūēre later.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The syncopated perfect adiēre maintains the elevated poetic register characteristic of Ovidian epic narrative."

notes.label: Syncopated Perfect
notes.body: Another syncopated perfect, but note who performs the action: serae — the bars themselves. Not "people barred the doors" but "bars shut the houses." The buildings themselves seem actively hostile, making the rejection feel more absolute.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The syncopated clausēre continues the elevated register, while serae as subject emphasises the active, hostile nature of the rejection."

notes.label: Pivotal Conjunction
notes.body: A single word carries the entire narrative pivot. After a thousand rejections, tamen signals everything changes. One house was different. The brevity of the pivot — just one word — makes it more powerful than any elaboration could.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The adversative tamen marks the crucial narrative pivot from universal rejection to singular welcome, creating suspense and highlighting the exceptional hospitality to follow."

notes.label: Concessive
notes.body: Ovid is upfront about the cottage's poverty. The concessive quidem ("admittedly") prepares for contrast: physical modesty will be offset by moral generosity. The honesty about the cottage's limitations makes the warmth inside it more striking.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The emphatic parva quidem acknowledges material poverty while the concessive quidem prepares for the moral contrast — physical modesty paired with spiritual abundance."

notes.label: Adversative
notes.body: After describing the cottage's humble exterior, sed swings us to what really matters: the people inside. The physical description is done. Now comes the character introduction that makes this story special.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The adversative sed signals the transition from physical setting to moral characterisation, establishing the thematic contrast between material poverty and spiritual wealth."

notes.label: Moral Epithet
notes.body: Pia is the highest Roman moral commendation — duty to the gods, to family, and to guests. Applying it to Baucis at her introduction tells the reader immediately: this woman is one of the good ones. Her pietas will earn divine favour.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The epithet pia immediately establishes Baucis's moral character. Her pietas contrasts with the impietas of the hostile neighbours and foreshadows her salvation."

notes.label: Named Subjects
notes.body: After the anonymity of "a thousand houses," Ovid finally gives us names. These two individuals stand out precisely because everyone else has been faceless. Naming them personalises the story and signals their importance.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The naming of Baucis and Philēmōn individualises the couple against the anonymous mīlle domōs. The Greek names provide local colour for this Phrygian setting."

notes.label: Ablative of Description
notes.body: Two words conveying a lifetime of partnership. Matched in age, matched in everything. The ablative of description packs biographical detail into the briefest possible space — characteristic of Ovid's economy. The equality here anticipates the final line's antithesis.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The ablative of description parīlī aetāte economically establishes the couple's lifelong partnership, emphasising their shared journey and mutual devotion."

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.trans: in that cottage… in that cottage
notes.body: The same word repeated — that cottage, that cottage — drums home the couple's rootedness. They married there, grew old there; their whole life is in one small, unchanged place. The anaphora creates a rhythm of contentment.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The anaphora illā… illā emphasises the cottage as the complete setting for their shared life, reinforcing themes of constancy and humble contentment."

notes.label: Compound Verb
notes.body: The con- prefix ("together, jointly") carries the emotional weight. They did not just age — they aged as one. A single syncopated perfect quietly contains their entire shared history.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The compound cōnsenūēre, with its con- prefix emphasising joint action, encapsulates the couple's lifelong partnership in a single syncopated perfect."

notes.label: Syncopated Perfect
notes.body: A fourth syncopated perfect (effēcērunt → effēcēre), framed by two ablative gerunds — fatendō ("by acknowledging") and ferendō ("by bearing"). It is not wealth but attitude that makes their poverty levem ("light"): contentment is presented as a deliberate act, not an accident of circumstance.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The syncopated perfect effēcēre, framed by the gerunds fatendō and ferendō, conveys that the couple actively render their poverty bearable through honest acceptance — defining contentment as a moral choice rather than a misfortune."

notes.label: Hyperbole
notes.trans: the two are the whole house
notes.body: A proper Roman household would have dozens of people — master, slaves, freedmen, clients. Here? Just Baucis and Philemon. Calling them tōta domus is playfully grand, contrasting the language of a great household with the reality of two people in a cottage.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The phrase tōta domus duo sunt employs gentle hyperbole, contrasting modest reality with the language of a grand Roman household while emphasising the couple's self-sufficiency."

notes.label: Emphatic Pronoun
notes.body: There is no distinction between who serves and who is served. In a normal Roman household, hierarchies were rigid. Here, Baucis and Philemon are simultaneously masters and servants. Īdem squashes all those distinctions into equality.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The emphatic pronoun īdem underscores the collapse of hierarchical distinctions — the couple simultaneously occupy roles that would be separate in a conventional household."

notes.label: Antithesis
notes.body: They obey and command — a paradox. In Rome these roles were rigidly separate. Baucis and Philemon have dissolved that hierarchy into a partnership of equals. The -que… -que polysyndeton links opposites into one seamless relationship — a witty, epigrammatic ending.
notes.exam: In an exam: "The antithetical pairing pārentque iubentque, linked by polysyndeton, creates a memorable paradox encapsulating the couple's egalitarian relationship and closes the introduction with epigrammatic wit."
